text: In mathematics, a Nikodym set is a subset of the unit square in ℝ² with a complement of Lebesgue measure zero (i.e., area 1), such that for any point in the set, there exists a straight line that intersects the set only at that point. The existence of such a set was first established by Otto Nikodym in 1927. Later, constructions were developed showing that each point in a Nikodym set has continuum many exceptional lines, and Kenneth Falconer identified analogues of these sets in higher dimensions. Nikodym sets are closely related to Kakeya sets, also known as Besicovitch sets. The existence of Nikodym sets is sometimes compared to the Banach–Tarski paradox, although a key difference exists: the Banach–Tarski paradox depends on non-measurable sets. Researchers have also studied Nikodym sets over finite fields, as opposed to ℝ.
